newsitem.title: GERMANY: German official sees intensive Bonn-Paris talks.
newsitem.headline: German official sees intensive Bonn-Paris talks.

text.p: A foreign policy expert in German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government said on Sunday he expected the projected Socialist-led victory in France's elections to lead to more intensive talks over the course of European monetary union and European social issues.

"I would expect the debate that has already begun to take place over the direction of economic and social policies to intensify," Karl Lamers, a member of Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) party, told German radio.
Televised computer projections showed France's Socialist-led left-wing opposition was on course for a stunning parliamentary election triumph in Sunday's decisive second-round runoff.
"I do not expect any change," Lamers said of the relationship between Bonn and Paris when asked if expected any dramatic switch in policy from a socialist-led France.
"I am pleased that the Socialists at least will be strong enough to have the decisive voice in government," he said.

But he said discussions about the future of the single European currency, along with efforts by Germany and France to meet entry criteria for its start in 1999, would be a top issue as both nations sought to cut budget deficits to required levels.
Germany's main evening television newscast opened with a live report saying that French President Jacques Chirac had apparently lost his bid to give a "new elan" to his government.
"The French left has made it. It is approaching a veritable landslide victory," ARD correspondent Heiko Engelkes reported from Paris.
"President Chirac is the clear loser. He wanted to win a bit of room to manoeuvre, he wanted to get a new elan for his conservative majority. That has now failed."

Germans watched developments in the French campaign closely, especially since a dispute between the Bonn governemnt and the powerful Bundesbank central bank raised the possibility of a delay in the European Union's planned monetary union (EMU).

The prospect of a new French government less committed to tough cuts in social spending to meet the tough Maastricht criteria for EMU has opened a range of new possibilities in hitherto strictly pro-European Bonn.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-left government has itself brought the Maastricht criteria into question by suddenly asking the Bundesbank to revalue its vast gold and currency reserves to provide more funds to help to qualify for EMU.
